evidence.excerpt: Furniture upholstery cutting presents a combined order-batching and nesting problem: grouping production orders into cutting batches determines which piece sets must be nested together, directly affecting fabric utilisation. This paper studies a medium-sized furniture manufacturer in Vojvodina with 80 to 120 active orders per week and 14 fabric types. A two-stage optimisation framework is proposed: an order-batching model based on set-partitioning assigns orders to batches sharing the same fabric type and colour, and a simulated annealing nesting solver then generates the physical layouts. The interaction between batch size and nesting efficiency is characterised over eight weeks of production data: increasing average batch size from 6 to 14 orders raises nesting utilisation from 76.3% to 81.7% at the cost of an average order lateness increase of 0.8 days. A Pareto front illustrating this trade-off is presented, and a simple weighting rule for practitioners is proposed. The framework was piloted over four weeks, reducing average fabric waste from 22.1% to 17.4%.
